claim: 73 samples of D. melanogaster were assembled from 23 localities in North America and Europe.
source: We assembled 73 samples of D. melanogaster collected from 23 localities in North America and Europe (Supplementary file 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the manuscript with reference to supplementary materials.

claim: For 15 sampling localities, flies were collected in the spring and fall over the course of 1–6 years.
source: For 15 sampling localities, flies were collected in the spring and fall over the course of 1–6 years (Figure 1A).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pooled resequencing identified ~1.75M SNPs following quality control and filtering for read depth and average minor allele frequency (minor allele frequency > 0.01).
source: Pooled resequencing identified ~1.75M SNPs following quality control and filtering for read depth and average minor allele frequency (minor allele frequency > 0.01).
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the sequencing analysis.

claim: After a second filtering, ~775,000 SNPs were retained that have observed polymorphism in each population sampled.
source: We applied a second filtering and retained ~775,000 SNPs that have observed polymorphism in each population sampled.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of additional filtering.

claim: Samples cluster by locality and geography in principal component analysis.
source: Samples cluster by locality and geography (Figure 1C)
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PC two separates the eastern North America samples by latitude with a linear regression p=3*10−15, R2 = 0.84.
source: PC two separates the eastern North America samples by latitude (linear regression p=3*10−15, R2 = 0.84).
evidence: Statistical result directly stated in the text.

claim: No PC is associated with season, following correction for multiple testing.
source: No PC is associated with season, following correction for multiple testing, implying that the spatial differentiation dominates patterns of SNP variation across these samples.
evidence: Directly stated as a result of the PCA analysis.

claim: The observed genome-wide distribution of 'seasonal' p-values from the GLM model is not uniform and there is a pronounced excess of SNPs with low p-values.
source: We find that the observed genome-wide distribution of 'seasonal' p-values from this model is not uniform and there is a pronounced excess of SNPs with low p-values (Figure 2A).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At a p-value of ~4*10−3, which corresponds to the top 1%, the observed data have a greater number of seasonal SNPs than 96.8% of the permutations.
source: For example, at a p-value of ~4*10−3, which corresponds to the top 1% (Supplementary file 1B), the observed data have a greater number of seasonal SNPs than 96.8% of the permutations (Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical comparison to permutations stated in text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Seasonal SNPs identified by Bergland et al., 2014 are slightly enriched among the top 1% of SNPs identified using the GLM, relative to matched genomic controls, after excluding the overlapping Pennsylvanian populations (log2 odds ratio ± SD = 0.59 ± 0.37, pperm = 0.0512).
source: Seasonal SNPs identified by Bergland et al., 2014 are slightly enriched among the top 1% of SNPs identified using the GLM, relative to matched genomic controls, after excluding the overlapping Pennsylvanian populations (log2 odds ratio ± SD = 0.59 ± 0.37, pperm = 0.0512).
evidence: Statistical comparison to previous study stated with specific values.

claim: Top set of seasonally variable SNPs shift in frequency by ~4–8%.
source: Our top set of seasonally variable SNPs shift in frequency by ~4–8% (Figure 2C).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The ~4–8% seasonal frequency shifts correspond to effective selection coefficients of ~10–30% per season (~1–3% per generation assuming 10 generations per season).
source: Taken at face value, this corresponds to effective selection coefficients of ~10–30% per season (~1–3% per generation assuming 10 generations per season).
evidence: Calculation based on observed frequency shifts, stated in text.

claim: Chromosomes 2L and 3R have the greatest nominal enrichment of seasonal SNPs relative to permutations, with a mean increase of 30% (pperm﻿ = 0.06) and of 18% (pperm = 0.08), respectively.
source: Chromosomes 2L and 3R have the greatest nominal enrichment of seasonal SNPs relative to permutations, with a mean increase of 30% (pperm﻿ = 0.06) and of 18% (pperm = 0.08), respectively.
evidence: Statistical results stated in text.

claim: Enrichment is much lower for chromosomes 2R and 3L (−2 and 4%, pperm = 0.54 and pperm = 0.20, respectively).
source: Enrichment is much lower for chromosomes 2R and 3L (−2 and 4%, pperm = 0.54 and pperm = 0.20, respectively).
evidence: Statistical results stated in text.

claim: The variation of the seasonal signal across chromosomes is statistically significant (ANOVA, p<10−15).
source: The variation of the seasonal signal across chromosomes is statistically significant (ANOVA, p<10−15).
evidence: Statistical test result stated in text.

claim: Regions near inversion breakpoints (±0.5 Mb) on chromosomes 2L (inversion In(2L)t) are strongly enriched for seasonal SNPs (85% enrichment, pperm = 0.03).
source: We find that regions near inversion breakpoints (±0.5 Mb) on chromosomes 2L (85% enrichment, pperm = 0.03, inversion In(2L)t)
evidence: Statistical results stated in text.

claim: Regions near inversion breakpoints on chromosome 3L (inversion In(3L)Payne) are strongly enriched for seasonal SNPs (30% enrichment, pperm = 0.01).
source: and 3L (30% enrichment, pperm = 0.01, inversion In(3L)Payne) are strongly enriched for seasonal SNPs.
evidence: Statistical results stated in text.

claim: Regions within the three inversions on chromosome 3R (In(3R)Mo, In(3R)K, In(3R)Payne) are enriched for seasonal SNPs (26% enrichment, pperm = 0.05).
source: Regions within the three inversions on chromosome 3R (In(3R)Mo, In(3R)K, In(3R)Payne) are also enriched for seasonal SNPs (26% enrichment, pperm = 0.05).
evidence: Statistical results stated in text.

claim: No evidence was found for enrichment of seasonal SNPs associated with In(2R)NS as previously reported by Kapun et al., 2016.
source: We do not find evidence for enrichment of seasonal SNPs associated with In(2R)NS as previously reported by Kapun et al., 2016.
evidence: Stated as a negative result with citation to previous work.

claim: In regions outside inversions (excluding the 0.5 Mb flanking the inversions), the seasonal signal is weaker, with a 2.5% enrichment of seasonal SNPs (pperm = 0.31).
source: In these regions, the seasonal signal is weaker, with a 2.5% enrichment of seasonal SNPs (pperm = 0.31).
evidence: Statistical results stated in text.

claim: Among the polymorphisms that are in the top 1% of both seasonal and clinal GLMs (n = 115), 74% have parallel allele frequency change (greater than 100/100 matched controls; naive expectation: 50%).
source: Among the polymorphisms that are in the top 1% of both seasonal and clinal GLMs (n = 115), 74% have parallel allele frequency change (greater than 100/100 matched controls; naive expectation: 50%).
evidence: Statistical comparison to matched controls stated in text.

claim: For the top 1% of seasonal and clinal polymorphism in California populations, 70% have parallel allele frequency change (greater than 100/100 matched controls).
source: We found a clear signal of parallelism between seasonal and latitudinal variation in both the California and the Europe comparisons: for the top 1% of seasonal and clinal polymorphism, 70% and 63% have parallel allele frequency change, for California and Europe, respectively (greater than 100/100 and 99/100 matched controls; Figure 2E).
evidence: Statistical comparison to matched controls stated in text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For the top 1% of seasonal and clinal polymorphism in European populations, 63% have parallel allele frequency change (greater than 99/100 matched controls).
source: We found a clear signal of parallelism between seasonal and latitudinal variation in both the California and the Europe comparisons: for the top 1% of seasonal and clinal polymorphism, 70% and 63% have parallel allele frequency change, for California and Europe, respectively (greater than 100/100 and 99/100 matched controls; Figure 2E).
evidence: Statistical comparison to matched controls stated in text and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For the top 5% of clinal and seasonal SNPs (n = 2132), parallel allele frequency change is highest near inversion breakpoints on chromosomes 2L (92%, CI95: 87–96%) and 3R (86%, CI95: 78–93%).
source: For the top 5% of clinal and seasonal SNPs (n = 2132), parallel allele frequency change is highest near inversion breakpoints on chromosomes 2L and 3R (92%, CI95: 87–96%, and 86%, CI95: 78–93%, respectively)
evidence: Statistical results with confidence intervals stated in text.

claim: For the top 5% of clinal and seasonal SNPs, parallel allele frequency change inside the 2L inversion is 83% (CI95: 80–87%).
source: and inside the 2L inversion (83%, CI95: 80–87%; Figure 2F).
evidence: Statistical results with confidence intervals stated in text and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Parallelism is greatest overall around inversion breakpoints (concordance: 81%, CI95: 77–84%).
source: While parallelism is greatest overall around inversion breakpoints (concordance: 81%, CI95: 77–84%)
evidence: Statistical results with confidence intervals stated in text.

claim: Parallelism inside inversions is 70% (CI95: 67–73%).
source: and inside inversions (concordance: 70%, CI95: 67–73%)
evidence: Statistical results with confidence intervals stated in text.

claim: A statistically significant excess of latitudinal and seasonal parallelism is observed outside of inversions (concordance: 57%, CI95: 53–62%).
source: we also observe a statistically significant excess of latitudinal and seasonal parallelism outside of inversions (concordance: 57%, CI95: 53–62%).
evidence: Statistical results with confidence intervals stated in text.

claim: The majority of populations show a positive predictability score.
source: We find that the majority of populations show a positive predictability score (Figure 3A).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For populations with positive predictability scores, the concordance rate reaches 60–70% among SNPs passing a stringent joint significance threshold (top 0.1% in both models).
source: For these populations, the concordance rate reaches 60–70% among SNPs passing a stringent joint significance threshold (top 0.1% in both models).
evidence: Stated in text as a result of the leave-one-out analysis.

claim: Four of the 20 populations had negative predictability scores (Benton Harbor, Michigan 2014; Lancaster, Massachusetts 2012; Topeka, Kansas 2014; and Esparto, California 2012).
source: At the same time, intriguingly, we found that four of the 20 populations had negative predictability scores (Benton Harbor, Michigan 2014; Lancaster, Massachusetts 2012; Topeka, Kansas 2014; and Esparto, California 2012).
evidence: Directly stated in text.

claim: Collection method, substrate, and D. simulans contamination rates are not correlated with the genome-wide predictability score more than expected by chance.
source: None of these variables are correlated with the genome-wide predictability score more than expected by chance (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Latitude and longitude are not strong predictors of variation in genome-wide predictability score.
source: Latitude and longitude are also not strong predictors of variation in genome-wide predictability score (Figure 3B).
evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The number of hot spring days and number of cold fall days prior to sampling is significantly correlated with genome-wide predictability score.
source: We find that the only set of features of the population that is significantly correlated with genome-wide predictability score is the number of hot spring days and number of cold fall days prior to sampling.
evidence: Stated as the result of environmental model testing.

claim: The best fit thermal limit model explains 82.2% of the variation in genome-wide predictability scores.
source: The best fit thermal limit model explains 82.2% of the variation in genome-wide predictability scores (Figure 3C and E)
evidence: Statistical result stated in text and shown in Figures 3C and 3E.

claim: The best fit thermal limit model beats >99.5% of permutations (false discovery rate = 17%).
source: and beats >99.5% of permutations (false discovery rate = 17%) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical comparison to permutations stated in text and shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The thermal limits identified by the best-fit model are the number of days in the 2 weeks prior to spring sampling with maximum temperature above ~32°C and the number of days in the fall with minimum temperature below ~5°C.
source: Specifically, the thermal limits identified by this best-fit model are the number of days in the 2 weeks prior to spring sampling with maximum temperature above ~32°C and the number of days in the fall with minimum temperature below ~5°C.
evidence: Stated as the result of the thermal limit model analysis.

claim: The thermal limits of ~32°C and ~5°C roughly correspond to upper and lower thermal limits for flies.
source: These values roughly correspond to upper and lower thermal limits for flies (Hoffmann, 2010; Kellermann et al., 2012; Overgaard and MacMillan, 2017).
evidence: Stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Seasonal adaptation is a general phenomenon of temperate D. melanogaster populations, and not restricted to a single orchard, biogeographic region, or continent.
source: Specifically, we demonstrate that seasonal adaptation is a general phenomenon of temperate D. melanogaster populations, and not restricted to a single orchard (Linvilla Orchard, Media, Pennsylvania: Behrman et al., 2015; Bergland et al., 2014; Cogni et al., 2014; Schmidt and Conde, 2006), biogeographic region (East Coast of North America: Behrman et al., 2018), or even a continent.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion with citations to previous work.

claim: Seasonal adaptation across the range is at least partly driven by a consistent set of loci.
source: By detecting consistent seasonal changes in allele frequencies among multiple populations in North America and Europe, we can argue that seasonal adaptation across this whole range is at least partly driven by a consistent set of loci.
evidence: Stated as an inference from the observed parallel seasonal changes.

claim: Inversions are important drivers of seasonal adaptation.
source: We detected stronger seasonal signal near or inside inversions on chromosomes 2L, 3L, and 3R, suggesting that inversions are important drivers of seasonal adaptation (Dobzhansky, 1948; Dobzhansky, 1943; Kapun et al., 2016; Kapun and Flatt, 2019; Rodríguez-Trelles et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the enrichment results with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Seasonal adaptation in D. melanogaster cannot involve wholesale population replacements by migration because the spatial structure of the D. melanogaster populations is robust year after year.
source: However, it is clear that seasonal adaptation in D. melanogaster cannot involve wholesale population replacements by migration because the spatial structure of the D. melanogaster populations is robust year after year as evidenced by strong spatial population structure (Figure 1C) and persistent clinal patterns (Machado et al., 2016; van Heerwaarden and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: Stated as an inference from observed population structure with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Exposure to temperature extremes, or to associated environmental variables, acts as a selective pressure in the wild, causing large fluctuations in allele frequency throughout the genome.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that exposure to temperature extremes, or to associated environmental variables, acts as a selective pressure in the wild, causing large fluctuations in allele frequency throughout the genome.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the thermal limit model results.

claim: When reared in a common laboratory environment, flies collected in winter or spring show higher stress tolerance compared to flies collected in the fall.
source: When reared in a common laboratory environment, flies collected in winter or spring (close descendants of flies that successfully overwintered) show higher stress tolerance (Behrman et al., 2015)
evidence: Stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: When reared in a common laboratory environment, flies collected in winter or spring show greater propensity to enter reproductive dormancy compared to flies collected in the fall.
source: greater propensity to enter reproductive dormancy (Schmidt and Conde, 2006)
evidence: Stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: When reared in a common laboratory environment, flies collected in winter or spring show increased innate immune function compared to flies collected in the fall.
source: increased innate immune function (Behrman et al., 2018)
evidence: Stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: When reared in a common laboratory environment, flies collected in winter or spring show modulated cuticular hydrocarbon profiles compared to flies collected in the fall.
source: and modulated cuticular hydrocarbon profiles (Rajpurohit et al., 2017) as compared to flies collected in the fall (the descendants of those flies who prospered during the summer).
evidence: Stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: A large number of common polymorphisms change in frequency over seasonal time scales in one mid-latitude orchard.
source: Genome-wide analysis indicated that a large number of common polymorphisms change in frequency over seasonal time scales in one mid-latitude orchard (Bergland et al., 2014)
evidence: Stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Allele frequency change among seasons has been observed using candidate gene approaches.
source: and allele frequency change among seasons has been observed using candidate gene approaches (Cogni et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Adaptively oscillating polymorphisms have been linked to seasonally varying phenotypes.
source: In several cases, these adaptively oscillating polymorphisms have been linked to seasonally varying phenotypes (Behrman et al., 2018; Erickson et al., 2020; Paaby et al., 2014).
evidence: Stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Seasonal adaptation was first observed in D. pseudoobscura by Dobzhansky and colleagues by tracking frequencies of inversion polymorphisms over seasons.
source: Seasonal adaptation was first observed in D. pseudoobscura by Dobzhansky and colleagues (e.g., Dobzhansky, 1943) by tracking frequencies of inversion polymorphisms over seasons.
evidence: Stated with citation to historical literature.

claim: Later studies confirmed and extended early findings on seasonal adaptation to other species including D. melanogaster and D. subobscura.
source: Later studies confirmed and extended these early findings to other species including D. melanogaster (Kapun et al., 2016; Stalker, 1980; Stalker, 1976) and D. subobscura (Rodríguez-Trelles et al., 2013).
evidence: Stated with citations to supporting literature.

claim: A population genetic model by Wittmann et al., 2017 has demonstrated that seasonally varying selection can maintain fitness-related genetic variation at many loci throughout the genome provided that dominance shifts from season to season.
source: For instance, a population genetic model by Wittmann et al., 2017 has demonstrated that seasonally varying selection can indeed maintain fitness-related genetic variation at many loci throughout the genome provided that dominance shifts from season to season in such a way that, on average, the seasonally favored allele remains slightly dominant (Curtsinger et al., 1994).
evidence: Stated with citations to theoretical literature.

claim: Classic quantitative genetic theory suggests that an optimal, plastic genotype will eventually dominate a population that is exposed to periodically changing environments.
source: Classic quantitative genetic theory suggests that an optimal, plastic genotype will eventually dominate a population that is exposed to periodically changing environments (Bürger and Gimelfarb, 1999; Korol et al., 1996; Lande, 2008; Scheiner, 1993).
evidence: Stated with citations to theoretical literature.

claim: Predictions from traditional population genetic models suggest that periodically changing environments will lead to the rapid loss of seasonally favored ecotypes.
source: Predictions from traditional population genetic models suggest that periodically changing environments will lead to the rapid loss of seasonally favored ecotypes as slight changes in selection pressure from one year to another eventually push allele frequencies at causal alleles to fixation (Hedrick, 1976).
evidence: Stated with citation to theoretical literature.

claim: For each sample, an average of 75 male flies were collected using direct aspiration from substrate, netting, or trapping at orchards and residential areas.
source: For each sample, members of the Drosophila Real-Time Evolution Consortium (DrosRTEC) collected an average of 75 male flies using direct aspiration from substrate, netting, or trapping at orchards and residential areas.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Paired-end 125 bp libraries were sequenced to an average of 94× coverage.
source: Paired-end 125 bp libraries were sequenced to an average of 94× coverage either at the Stanford Sequencing Service Center on an Illumina HiSeq 2000 or at the Stanford Functional Genomics facility on an Illumina HiSeq 4000.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: For the populations used in this analysis, the average proportion of reads mapping preferentially to D. simulans was less than 1%.
source: For the populations used in this analysis, the average proportion of reads mapping preferentially to D. simulans was less than 1% (see Supplementary file 1)
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: There was no significant difference in the level of D. simulans contamination between spring and fall samples (t-test p=0.90).
source: and there was no significant difference in the level of D. simulans contamination between spring and fall samples (t-test p=0.90).
evidence: Statistical test result stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: In silico simulation analysis shows that competitive mapping accurately estimates the fraction of D. simulans contamination.
source: In silico simulation analysis shows that competitive mapping accurately estimates the fraction of D. simulans contamination.
evidence: Stated as a result of simulation analysis in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Simulations demonstrate that the estimation of the cross species mapping is precise (Pearson's r = 0.9999, p=1.6×10−24), but underestimates the true contamination rate by ~2%.
source: These simulations demonstrate that the estimation of the cross species mapping is precise (Pearson's r = 0.9999, p=1.6×10−24), but underestimates the true contamination rate by ~2%.
evidence: Statistical results from simulation stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The Core20 set is composed of 20 pairs of spring and fall samples from the same location.
source: The first subset ('Core20') is composed of 20 pairs of spring and fall samples from the same location.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Samples in the Core20 set are drawn from 15 localities in North America and Europe.
source: Samples in the Core20 set are drawn from 15 localities in North America and Europe and we use at most 2 years of sampling from any one locality.
evidence: Directly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The Clinal subset consists of four populations sampled in the spring along the East Coast of North America.
source: The second subset of samples ('Clinal') was used to examine patterns of clinal variation along the East Coast of North America and consists of four populations sampled in the spring (see Materials and methods and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly stated in the Results section.

claim: The strength of selection implied by the magnitude of fluctuations at seasonal sites is likely to be an underestimate.
source: While the number of detected seasonal loci is likely to be a vast overestimate of the number of causal seasonal variants, particularly if there is selection on large inversions, the strength of selection implied by the magnitude of fluctuations at seasonal sites is likely to be an underestimate.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: Partially linked loci should show a smaller magnitude of fluctuation than the true causal sites.
source: Partially linked loci should show a smaller magnitude of fluctuation than the true causal sites.
evidence: Stated as a theoretical expectation in the Discussion section.

claim: The 4–8% seasonal frequency shifts at the top 1% of the seasonal sites and the corresponding effective selection coefficients of ~10–30% per season (~1–3% per generation) imply even larger magnitudes of selection at the causal sites.
source: Thus the 4–8% seasonal frequency shifts at the top 1% of the seasonal sites and the corresponding effective selection coefficients of ~10–30% per season (~1–3% per generation) imply even larger magnitudes of selection at the causal sites.
evidence: Stated as an inference from the observed data in the Discussion section.

claim: Seasonal selection force could rival in strength genetic draft due to selective sweeps and should be much stronger over seasonal timescales than random genetic drift in populations as large as D. melanogaster.
source: This seasonal selection force could rival in strength genetic draft due to selective sweeps and should be much stronger over seasonal timescales than random genetic drift in populations as large as D. melanogaster (Karasov et al., 2010).
evidence: Stated as an interpretation with citation to supporting literature.

claim: The most straightforward explanation of the observation of signals of seasonal adaptation at common SNPs is that these polymorphisms are subject to balancing selection.
source: The most straightforward explanation of these results is that these polymorphisms are subject to balancing selection (Bertram and Masel, 2019; Charlesworth, 2015; Gulisija and Kim, 2015, Levene, 1953; Wittmann et al., 2017).
evidence: Stated as an interpretation with citations to theoretical literature.

claim: Pervasive balancing selection is consistent with the recent realization that simple models of mutation-selection balance are inconsistent with the extent of quantitative genetic variation in a variety of fitness-related traits.
source: Pervasive balancing selection is consistent with the recent realization that simple models of mutation-selection balance are inconsistent with the extent of quantitative genetic variation in a variety of fitness-related traits (Charlesworth, 2015).
evidence: Stated with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Natural selection may not push populations in the same consistent direction across the entire growing season but rather may be more heterogeneous through time.
source: These findings also raise an intriguing possibility that natural selection may not push populations in the same consistent direction across the entire growing season but rather that natural selection and adaptation may be more heterogeneous through time (Grant, 2002; Nosil et al., 2020; Siepielski et al., 2009).
evidence: Stated as an interpretation with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Evolution and ecology do operate on similar timescales in this system.
source: Our results thus illustrate that evolution and ecology do operate on similar timescales in this system (Hendry, 2020; Schoener, 2011; Thompson, 1998; Yoshida et al., 2003)
evidence: Stated as a conclusion with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Evolutionary adaptation cannot be generally ignored a priori in demographic or ecological investigations even on extremely short timescales.
source: and that evolutionary adaptation cannot be generally ignored a priori in demographic or ecological investigations even on extremely short timescales (Rudman et al., 2018).
evidence: Stated as a conclusion with citation to supporting literature.

claim: The detected seasonal SNPs can either be causal or, vastly more likely, linked to nearby causal genetic variants.
source: The detected seasonal SNPs can either be causal or, vastly more likely, linked to nearby causal genetic variants, be they SNPs, indels, structural variants, or transposable element insertions.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation in the Discussion section.

claim: The power to detect parallel seasonal evolution should be stronger for regions with reduced recombination.
source: Furthermore, the power to detect parallel seasonal evolution should be stronger for regions with reduced recombination, plausibly increasing the power of our approach to detect parallel adaptation linked to structural variants.
evidence: Stated as a theoretical expectation in the Discussion section.

claim: The complicated architecture of seasonal adaptation will require a much broader seasonal sampling of populations to fine-map the causal variants.
source: Thus, our study suggests that the complicated architecture of seasonal adaptation will require a much broader seasonal sampling of populations to fine-map the causal variants and that such an endeavor is not futile, given that it is possible to detect a set of loci that show consistent seasonal fluctuations with all the limitation of the approach notwithstanding.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion and recommendation in the Discussion section.

claim: It is important in the future to obtain genomic data capable of identifying structural variation, including inversions, that plausibly underlie much of seasonal adaptation in Drosophila.
source: It is also clearly important in the future to obtain genomic data capable of identifying structural variation, including inversions, that plausibly underlie much of seasonal adaptation in Drosophila.
evidence: Stated as a recommendation in the Discussion section.

claim: The spatial structure of the D. melanogaster populations is robust year after year as evidenced by strong spatial population structure and persistent clinal patterns.
source: However, it is clear that seasonal adaptation in D. melanogaster cannot involve wholesale population replacements by migration because the spatial structure of the D. melanogaster populations is robust year after year as evidenced by strong spatial population structure (Figure 1C) and persistent clinal patterns (Machado et al., 2016; van Heerwaarden and Hoffmann, 2007).
evidence: Stated with reference to data and citations to supporting literature.

claim: Generic selective pressures that drive seasonal adaptation must both shift between seasons locally and vary spatially from south to north.
source: The seasonal and latitudinal parallelism in allele frequency change that we observe (Figure 2E) suggests that the environmental factors that drive these patterns must both shift between seasons locally and vary spatially from south to north.
evidence: Stated as an inference from the observed parallelism.

claim: At the time of sampling, some spring samples had already experienced sufficiently strong selection in the generically summer way and fall samples had experienced selective pressures in the generically winter way.
source: We thus hypothesize that, at the time of sampling, some of our spring samples had already experienced sufficiently strong selection in the generically summer way and that the fall samples had experienced selective pressures in the generically winter way.
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis to explain the observed patterns.

claim: The elevated signal of parallelism between spatial and seasonal allele frequency fluctuations across the whole genome, and in particular outside of inverted regions, suggests that inversions themselves, while important, are not the sole drivers of allele frequency change between seasons.
source: The elevated signal of parallelism between spatial and seasonal allele frequency fluctuations across the whole genome, and in particular outside of inverted regions, suggests that inversions themselves, while important, are not the sole drivers of allele frequency change between seasons.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the parallelism results.

claim: The Bayenv analysis shows substantial overlap with the GLM set, with 20% of the top 1% of SNPs in the GLM analysis also in the top 1% of the Bayenv analysis, compared with a naive expectation of 1%.
source: Specifically, for the top 1% of SNPs in the GLM analysis, 20% are also in the top 1% of the Bayenv analysis, compared with a naive expectation of 1% (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statistical comparison stated in text and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.
